rows.subtype: Approach: researching market ranges and gathering evidence [Thinking]
rows.description: Before an offer discussion, a developer checks salary ranges for similar roles in Pune, talks to peers, and lists her skills. She sets a target and a minimum she will accept.

rows.subtype: Approach: deciding the walk-away point beforehand [Thinking]
rows.description: He decides in advance the lowest total package he would take and what else matters, such as remote days and learning budget. This stops him from agreeing under pressure.

rows.subtype: Approach: accepting the first offer from fear of losing it [Pitfall]
rows.description: Afraid the offer will vanish, she says yes immediately. Later she learns colleagues at the same level were paid more, and she regrets not asking even one question.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing the outcome and preparing for the next round [Revision]
rows.description: After settling slightly below target, she notes what worked and sets a review date with her manager. She plans measurable results to support a stronger request next time.

rows.subtype: Approach: triage of topics by marks and confidence [Thinking]
rows.description: With thirty days left, a student rates each topic by exam weight and self-confidence, and decides to revise high-weight, medium-confidence topics first, since they give the biggest gain per hour.

rows.subtype: Approach: backward calendar with buffer days [Action]
rows.description: The student writes the exam dates, subtracts rest days, assigns each subject revision blocks, and keeps the last two days before each paper for light review and sleep rather than new material.

rows.subtype: Approach: trying to relearn everything from scratch [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student starts again from Chapter 1 of every book. By week three only half the syllabus has been touched, and the final chapters, often heavily weighted, are hurried or skipped.

rows.subtype: Approach: mid-month check and cutting low-yield topics [Revision]
rows.description: At the halfway point the student sees she is behind by four chapters. She drops rarely asked topics with the teacher's agreement and reallocates hours to areas that appear in every past paper.

rows.subtype: Approach: defining a minimum viable version first [Thinking]
rows.description: A group of students planning a school notes-sharing site decides that version one is just a page with uploaded PDFs sorted by subject, leaving accounts and ratings for later.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition and dividing roles [Action]
rows.description: Three teens split a website project into design, content and coding, write who does what and by when on a shared sheet, and meet twice weekly for ten minutes to check progress.

rows.subtype: Approach: overbuilding features before anyone uses it [Pitfall]
rows.description: A teen adds chat, badges and a dark mode to her app before sharing it, runs out of exam-free weeks, and launches nothing, while classmates only wanted a simple timetable page.

rows.subtype: Approach: iterating from feedback and usage numbers [Revision]
rows.description: A teen notices from simple visit counts that no one opens the third page, asks why, learns it is hard to find, moves it to the homepage, and checks that visits rise.

rows.subtype: Approach: tracking every expense for two months [Thinking]
rows.description: A couple records all spending in a shared app and finds that food delivery and subscriptions take a fifth of their income. The finding is a surprise that reshapes their plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising debts by interest rate [Thinking]
rows.description: With a credit card balance and a low interest education loan, they clear the high interest card first while paying minimum on the loan. Order matters more than small extra payments everywhere.

rows.subtype: Approach: strict budgeting that collapses in month three [Pitfall]
rows.description: A very tight plan with no fun money works for weeks, then one outing breaks it. Feeling they failed, the couple abandons the budget, showing that rigidity can undermine consistency.

rows.subtype: Approach: revising categories after an income change [Revision]
rows.description: When a salary hike arrives, they resist raising spending and split it into higher savings, a small lifestyle upgrade and a parents' support fund, and rewrite the plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: copying rules from a game they already know [Thinking]
rows.description: A group of children design a new game on the terrace by borrowing from kabaddi and tag. Using known rules gives them a working start without inventing everything from nothing.

rows.subtype: Approach: playing a quick trial round to test it [Action]
rows.description: The children try the game for five minutes without fixing every rule. They notice the same fast runner always wins, so they add a rule that runners must hop for the last few steps.

rows.subtype: Approach: making many complicated rules before playing [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy writes twenty rules on paper before anyone plays. His friends lose interest while listening, and forget half the rules, and they drift off to play something else.

rows.subtype: Approach: adapting the game for the youngest player [Revision]
rows.description: A six-year-old cousin keeps getting out first and starts to cry. The older children add a safe zone where little ones cannot be caught, so everybody can stay in the game.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing goals and time horizon [Thinking]
rows.description: When the market falls twenty percent, a young investor asks when the money is needed. Funds meant for retirement decades away are treated differently from money for a house in two years.

rows.subtype: Approach: rebalancing by written rule [Action]
rows.description: Following a plan made earlier, the investor moves a small share from stable assets into equity when the mix drifts, using a rule set in a calm period rather than emotion.

rows.subtype: Approach: panic selling at the bottom [Pitfall]
rows.description: Watching daily losses and social media fear, the investor sells everything to stop the pain. Later recovery happens without them, and the loss becomes permanent.

rows.subtype: Approach: learning from a past drawdown [Revision]
rows.description: Recalling that a smaller fall two years earlier was recovered, the investor reviews notes from that time and sticks with the plan, but lowers exposure to one risky sector.
